text: Over the course of the war, drones went from being scarce and quickly lost to being the main killer on the battlefield.
notes: Uncited synthesis in the overview; cites the overview's sources for the start and end points as background.

text: In 2022 drones were mostly scouts: commercial quadcopters, Ukrainian fixed-wing ISR drones and a few Bayraktar TB2s.
Around 90% of Ukrainian UAVs were lost in 2022.
Only about a third of Ukrainian UAV missions succeeded in 2022.

metric_new.label: Share of UAV missions judged successful

text: The Russian Shahed drone campaign against Ukrainian cities began in late September 2022.
In 2023 Russia's 'reconnaissance-fires circuit' of Orlan-10 drones plus artillery, and the Lancet loitering munition, dominated the battlefield.
By autumn 2023 Russian Lancets were hitting Ukrainian jets about 65 km from Russian-held ground.
In 2023 Ukraine was losing about 10,000 UAVs a month to Russian electronic warfare (EW).
The FPV (first-person-view kamikaze quadcopter) boom arrived in 2024.
RUSI's fieldwork found that tactical UAVs caused 60–70% of damaged or destroyed Russian systems in 2024.
RUSI's fieldwork found that 60–80% of FPVs never reached their target in 2024.
Russian Shahed-type launches roughly tripled in 2024 compared with 2023, to about 11,000, most of them after August.
In 2025 a drone 'kill zone' 10–15 km deep formed on both sides of the line.
The Drone Line project, announced in February 2025, was one driver of the 2025 kill zone.
Fibre-optic FPVs with 40+ km reach helped form the 2025 kill zone.
Russia's Rubikon center hunting Ukrainian drone teams and logistics helped form the 2025 kill zone.
Russia launched over 50,000 Shahed-type drones at Ukraine in 2025.
Ukraine was mass-producing interceptor drones at about 950 a day by December 2025.
Russia lost access to Starlink in early February 2026: ISW dates it to 1 February and the Kyiv Independent to 5 February.
The Starlink loss in February 2026 grounded Russia's deeper-reaching strike drones but not its fibre-optic FPVs.
Because Russia's fibre-optic FPVs were unaffected by the Starlink loss, the close kill zone kept growing, to 20–25 km in some sectors by July 2026.
In 2026 Ukrainian ground robots (UGVs) took over a large share of front-line logistics.
In 2026 Russia moved to jet-powered Gerans, which are much harder to intercept.
Ukrainian officials claim drones cause 70–80% of Russian casualties.
In December 2025 Ukrainian drone units reportedly 'neutralised' about as many Russians as Russia recruited.
notes: Claimant is Syrskyi per the passage in 01/0022 and the source id.

text: In Feb–Apr 2022 both sides used commercial and adapted quadcopters at tactical level and fixed-wing ISR drones at medium altitude: Ukraine's SKIF, Leleka and Furia, and Russia's Orlan-10.
In Feb–Apr 2022 Ukraine flew Bayraktar TB2s and Russia flew Orion MALE (medium-altitude, long-endurance) drones, committed only under favourable conditions.
Ukrainian battalions had been receiving Furia, Leleka and PD-1 UAVs since 2015.
Linking Furia, Leleka and PD-1 UAVs to the Kropyva fire-control software sped up Ukrainian artillery engagements.
Deviro dates formal adoption of the Leleka to 2019.
Athlon Avia dates formal adoption of the Furia to 2020, after state trials.
Ukrainian UAV attrition in Feb–Apr 2022 was extreme: about 90% of Ukrainian UAVs were destroyed.
In early 2022 a Ukrainian quadcopter survived about 3 flights and a fixed-wing UAV about 6.

metric_new.label: UAV life expectancy (flights or sorties before loss)
UAV life expectancy (flights or sorties before loss)

text: In early 2022 only about 1/3 of Ukrainian UAV missions succeeded.

metric_new.label: Share of UAV missions judged successful

text: FPV kamikaze drones barely existed in 2022: Ukraine had about 3,000–5,000 FPVs that year.

observations.subject: FPV drones
observations.note: Text says Ukraine 'had'; key-figures table calls it output

text: The Orlan-10 was the Russian workhorse drone in May–Aug 2022.
In 2022 Russian units with their own UAVs could fire within 3–5 minutes of detection, against 20–30 minutes when the request went through a fire-control headquarters.
Russia did not have enough Orlan-10s to sustain its loss rate in Donbas in 2022.
The Army of Drones (Armiia Droniv) programme launched in July 2022, run by UNITED24, the General Staff and the Ministry of Digital Transformation.

mentions.name: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine

text: Within its first 9 months the Army of Drones contracted 3,200 UAV complexes worth over UAH 4bn (about $107m).
Within its first 9 months the Army of Drones trained 7,000+ drone operators.
Russian use of the Lancet-3(M) loitering munition rose from about October 2022.
By early March 2023 Oryx had logged 113 visually confirmed Kub/Lancet hits and 41 misses, mostly on artillery, radars and SAM launchers.
The first Shahed-136/131 appears in Ukrainian Air Force reports on 28 September 2022.
At least 409 Shahed drones were launched at Ukraine from September to December 2022.
notes: The file notes these counts are floors because early reports often gave only the number destroyed.

text: Shahed launches peaked at 253 in October 2022.
The biggest Shahed night of 2022 was 19 December, with 35 drones.
About 95% of Shaheds launched in September–December 2022 were reported shot down.
Early Air Force reports often gave only the number of Shaheds destroyed, so the 2022 launch counts are floors.
Ukrspecsystems' Shark ISR drone was unveiled in October 2022 to spot for HIMARS under heavy EW.
The Shark ISR drone (2022) has a 60 km link, flies for 2+ hours at a cruising speed of 70–90 km/h and weighs 10 kg.
The Shark-M, the Shark's 2026 successor, flies for up to 7 hours on a 180 km link.
During the Bakhmut period (Dec 2022–May 2023) Russia had at least one major EW system per 10 km of front.

metric_new.label: EW system density along the front

observations.value_text: at least one major EW system per 10 km of front
observations.note: major EW systems per 10 km of front

text: During the Bakhmut period Ukrainian UAV losses stayed at about 10,000 a month.
In Dec 2022–May 2023 Russian counter-battery fire shifted from area saturation to Lancet strikes.
In Dec 2022–May 2023 Russian Orlan-10 'complexes' orbited at both axis and artillery-brigade level.
In Dec 2022–May 2023 Russian Orlan-30s laser-designated targets for Krasnopol guided shells.
Shahed launches fell to about 240 in Q1 2023, with 45 in February.
Shahed launches jumped to 411 in May 2023 with the spring campaign on Kyiv.
During the 2023 counteroffensive Ukraine hit Russian reserves at night with converted agricultural drones dropping RPGs, the forerunners of the 'Baba Yaga' heavy bombers.
In one 2023 strike, 5 Ukrainian converted agricultural drones carrying 4 RPGs each destroyed or badly damaged 7 Russian tanks, and all 5 drones were lost.
The 2023 Ukrainian agricultural-drone night-bombing tactic was binary: it worked only when Russian EW lapsed.
In the 2023 counteroffensive Russia struck the lead elements of Ukrainian assaults with Lancets and FPVs flown together with ISR drones.
RUSI flagged improvements from the Lancet-3 to the Lancet-3M in 2023.
RUSI noted that in 2023 Ukrainian units had to train for up to 25 Russian UAVs watching them at once.

observations.subject: Russian UAVs observing a unit at once

text: In autumn 2023 Russian Lancets destroyed a MiG-29 and an Su-25 at Dovhyntseve airbase near Kryvyi Rih, about 65 km from Russian-held ground.
Lancet targets are found by Orlan-10 or Supercam drones and handed to a launcher team.
A newer Lancet model pre-detonates its shaped charge to defeat nets and cages.
The Lancet-3 weighs about 12 kg.
One Lancet-3 is estimated to cost about $35,000.
ZALA advertised the tube-launched Izdeliye-53 with 'fully autonomous' and swarm modes.
Russian channels claimed the first use of the Izdeliye-53 on 21 October 2023.
HUR spokesman Yusov said there was no evidence of mass use of the Izdeliye-53 (2023).
Russian Shahed launches ran at about 200–500 a month in 2023, with 685 in Q2 and 916 in Q3.
The Ukrainian Air Force reported about 82–87% of Shaheds shot down in mid-2023.

effect: defeats the tactic unless EW lapses
rationale: RUSI found the 2023 night-bombing tactic was binary and worked only when Russian EW lapsed.
A newer Lancet model pre-detonates its shaped charge to defeat nets and cages.

text: The Ukrainian FPV boom took off in Oct 2023–Jul 2024.
Ukraine built about 2.2 million UAVs of all types in 2024, according to OSW.
CSIS says Ukraine built 'approximately 2 million' UAVs in 2024, 96% of them domestic.
The defence minister's figures imply Ukraine received about 1.2 million FPVs in 2024, since he claimed 2025 was 2.5 times higher.
In 2024 Ukraine began buying 10,000 AI-enhanced drones, a small fraction of its drone output.
The Unmanned Systems Forces (Syly bezpilotnykh system, USF) became a separate branch of the Ukrainian armed forces in June 2024.
Shahed launches rose to 1,280 in Q4 2023, including a record 625 in December 2023.
Shahed launches were 1,294 in Q1 2024, then dipped to 973 in Q2 2024.
The biggest Shahed night of 2023 was 25 November, with 75 drones.
CSIS, using Ukrainian Air Force data, counts over 14,700 one-way attack drones launched at Ukraine from 28 September 2022 to the end of 2024, about 90% of them shot down.
CSIS takes $35,000 as the midpoint Shahed unit cost, with estimates ranging from $20,000 to $80,000.
CSIS's cost assumptions make about $350,000 of Shahed spending per target struck (2022–2024).
HUR puts the damage from Magura V5 strikes on Russian ships at over $500m.
RUSI's 2024 fieldwork found battlefield transparency dense within 3 km of the line, thinning out to 15 km, with targets taskable out to 40 km.
RUSI's 2024 fieldwork found armoured vehicles had to stay concealed or dug in within about 3 km of the line.

metric_new.label: Distance from the line kept by vehicles

observations.subject: armoured vehicles concealed or dug in

text: RUSI's 2024 fieldwork found excavators rarely came closer than 7 km to the line.

metric_new.label: Distance from the line kept by vehicles

text: RUSI's 2024 fieldwork found dedicated UAV units covered 40–70 km sections of front.

metric_new.label: Width of front covered per unit

text: RUSI's 2024 fieldwork found bomber drones did more damage than FPVs but mostly flew at night.
RUSI's 2024 fieldwork found about 50% of Ukrainian casualties were taken in the rear, from FPVs, artillery and glide bombs.

observations.subject: Ukrainian casualties taken in the rear

text: HUR says Magura V5 naval drones hit the Ivanovets, Tsezar Kunikov, Sergey Kotov, Ivan Khurs and several landing and patrol craft, the first three in Feb–Mar 2024.
notes: Ship names given as system mentions without a kind (no ship kind in vocab).

text: Russia founded the Rubikon center on 2 August 2024.
Rubikon systematically cut the supply lines to Ukrainian positions around Sudzha, which made the Kursk salient unsustainable.
Ukraine withdrew from the Kursk salient in March 2025.
RUSI noted Russia's shift to fibre-optic-guided FPVs, which cannot be jammed but have about 10 km range, fly worse and snag on obstacles.
RUSI noted that Ukraine 'does not yet widely employ' fibre-optic FPVs (early 2025).
Ukraine's answer to Russian jamming leaned on AI terminal guidance for FPVs.
CSIS found in early 2025 that most small FPV missions under jamming succeed only 10–15% of the time.

observations.subject: FPV under jamming, no terminal guidance

text: CSIS found in early 2025 that autonomous terminal navigation raises FPV mission success under jamming to 70–80%.
According to CSIS, with autonomous terminal navigation one or two FPVs do the work of eight or nine.
According to CSIS, FPV terminal-guidance lock-on range grew from 300 m to about 1 km, and 2 km in good conditions.
CSIS stresses that true drone autonomy is 'not yet present on the battlefield': a human still selects the target (early 2025).

cites.quote: not yet present on the battlefield

text: In August 2024 Russia flew 1,000–1,500 Orlan-10/Zala orbits a day over Ukraine.
From late 2024 radar-cued Ukrainian interceptor UAVs began wearing down Russian Orlan-10/Zala reconnaissance drones.
CSIS puts Russian Shahed launches at about 130 a week before September 2024 and about 1,100 a week by March 2025.
In monthly Air Force figures, Shahed launches went from 426 in July 2024 to 1,334 in September, 2,464 in November and 4,044 in March 2025.
From September to December 2024 Russia launched more Shahed-type drones than in the previous 23 months combined.
The reported Shahed shot-down share fell to 55–58% from Q4 2024 because the Air Force began counting drones 'lost' to EW separately.
Ukraine's Sting interceptor drone first appeared in autumn 2024.
HUR claims a missile-armed Magura V5 naval drone destroyed two Russian Mi-8 helicopters on 31 December 2024, the first such kill.

measure: RF jamming of drone control links
rationale: RUSI: fibre-optic-guided FPVs cannot be jammed, at the price of range (~10 km early 2025), flight performance and snagging.

measure: RF jamming of drone control links
effect: raises success under jamming from 10–15% to a claimed 70–80%
rationale: CSIS: autonomous terminal navigation raises FPV success under jamming from 10–15% to 70–80%.
RUSI: radar-cued interceptor UAVs began wearing down Russian Orlan/Zala orbits.

text: The Ukrainian Defence Ministry announced the Drone Line (Liniia droniv) on 9 February 2025.
The Drone Line groups five elite units: the K-2, Achilles and Rarog regiments, Magyar's Birds (414th brigade) and the Border Guard's Phoenix.
The Drone Line's aim is a kill zone 10–15 km deep.
The Defence Ministry's anniversary material dates the start of Drone Line operations to March 2025; sources dating it to 'spring' or June describe later steps.
The Defence Ministry puts the cost of the Drone Line at $880m.
On 20 June 2025 the USF and the Drone Line units were placed under one command group.
Robert 'Magyar' Brovdi took command of the Unmanned Systems Forces on 3 June 2025.
According to Fedorov, Ukrainian fibre-optic FPVs went from about 20 km to 40+ km range between spring and July 2025.
ISW says Russian fibre-optic FPVs reach up to 60 km.
Russia's plywood Molniya fixed-wing drone strikes Ukrainian logistics 50+ km deep.
Molniya variants carry an FPV, run on fibre, or carry Starlink for reconnaissance.
In spring 2025 Rubikon had 7 units of 130–150 people.
By September 2025 over 25% of Rubikon's strikes were on Ukrainian drone teams and 15% on EW.

observations.subject: Rubikon strikes on Ukrainian drone teams

text: Rubikon grew to about 5,000 personnel by spring 2026.
In Operation Spiderweb (Pavutyna) on 1 June 2025, 117 FPVs were launched from trucks at Russian bomber bases.
The SBU and General Staff claim Operation Spiderweb hit 41 Russian aircraft and caused about $7bn in damage.

claimants.name: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine

text: The Liutyi long-range drone's range doubled to about 1,000 km (2025).
The Liutyi costs as little as $55,000.
Fewer than 30% of Liutyi drones reach the target area (2025).
The SBU claims 160+ drone strikes on Russian oil facilities in 2025.
Russia launched 54,538 Shahed-type drones at Ukraine in 2025.
About 40% of the Shahed-type drones Russia launched in 2025 were decoys.
The record Shahed night of 2025 was 7 September, with 810 drones.
The compiled Air Force reports give 54,800 Shahed-type launches for 2025, near-identical to the ISIS count.
July 2025 set a monthly Shahed launch record of 6,129, against 423 in July 2024.
notes: The compiled Air Force series (01/0020) gives 426 for July 2024.

text: The Shahed hit rate rose from 2–3% early in 2025 to about 17% in December 2025.
The jet-powered Geran-3 appeared in 2025, and the Geran-4/5 followed in late 2025.
The Sting interceptor drone reaches over 315 km/h and costs about $2,000.
Sting's maker reports 60–90% efficiency against Shahed-type drones and says 8 in 10 kills need only one interceptor.

observations.subject: Sting kills needing only one interceptor

notes: The maker is not named in the text; the claim is self-reported.

text: Ukrainian interceptor drone deliveries reached about 950 a day in December 2025.
Swarmer's software had flown 'over a hundred' swarm missions by September 2025, in which drones in a group decide which strikes first.
Brave1's AI lead put a simple AI targeting kit for drones at about $150 (2025).
notes: Claimant is Brave1's AI lead, unnamed in the text.

text: Brave1's AI lead said the share of UAVs hitting targets without AI targeting 'is constantly decreasing' (2025).
Russia's V2U drone was seen flying in groups of six with onboard AI and a 4G modem (2025).
Russian hexacopter copies of the Vampire heavy bomber, also called 'Baba Yaga', appeared in 2025.
The Ukrainian 81st Brigade says it had shot down five Russian Vampire copies by March 2026.
HUR claims a Magura V5 missile shot down an Su-30 near Novorossiysk on 2 May 2025.
An SBU source says SBU Sea Baby drones disabled the empty shadow-fleet tankers Kairos and Virat off Turkey on 28 November 2025, in a joint operation with the Navy.
The SBU says its underwater Sea Baby put a Russian Kilo-class submarine out of service in Novorossiysk on 15 December 2025.
Under e-points (ye-baly) and the 'Army of Drones Bonus', Ukrainian units upload confirmed hits to DELTA and spend the points on Brave1 Market.
Ukrainian units had ordered over UAH 5bn on Brave1 Market with e-points since August 2025.
notes: End date of the period is not stated; source is a 2025 official account.

text: Under e-points a killed Russian soldier was worth 2 points, then 6 from April 2025.
By January 2026 e-points valued a killed soldier at 12 points, a drone operator at 25 and a soldier captured alive at 120.
E-points prices move to steer the behaviour of Ukrainian units.
By mid-2026 e-points also paid for reconnaissance, logistics and evacuation missions.
Ukraine obtained 3 million FPVs in 2025.
Ukraine obtained about 15,000 UGVs in 2025.
OSW projected Ukrainian output of 4.5 million UAVs of all types in 2025.
Syrskyi claims Ukrainian USF units 'neutralised' about 33,000 Russians (video-confirmed) in December 2025.

rationale: Sting's maker reports 60–90% efficiency, 8 in 10 kills with one interceptor, at about $2,000 a drone.

text: SpaceX's whitelist cut Russian Starlink terminals in early February 2026.
ISW dates the Starlink block on Russian terminals to 1 February 2026.
The Kyiv Independent reported the front-wide Russian Starlink cut-off on 5 February 2026.
After the February 2026 cut-off, the larger Russian attack drones that struck 20–200 km deep via Starlink lost their link.
Russian FPVs on line-of-sight or mesh radio carried on after the February 2026 Starlink cut-off.
Russia had fitted Starlink on Shaheds, Molniyas and the BM-35.
One Ukrainian engineer estimates that only a 'single-digit percentage' of Russian drones used Starlink.
notes: The engineer is unnamed in the text.

text: 3rd Army Corps commander Biletsky says the Starlink outage cut the effectiveness of Russia's drone campaign by roughly 20–40% in two weeks.

observations.subject: Russian drone campaign
observations.note: reduction over the first two weeks

text: Biletsky expected partial recovery of Russian drone effectiveness within one to two months of the Starlink cut-off.
ISW saw lower tempo and depth in Russian tactical and mid-range drone strikes after the Starlink cut-off, only partly offset by local SIM cards and relay drones.
After the Starlink cut-off, Ukrainian counterattacks began across nine vectors toward Huliaipole and in Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts.
During the February 2026 counterattacks one up-armoured Ukrainian M1A1 was still immobilised by Russian FPVs.
Ukrainian brigades gave mixed accounts of how much Russian assaults actually slowed after the Starlink cut-off.
The Kyiv Independent's front reporting noted that Russia's dispersed infantry assaults hardly needed Starlink (2026).
After the Starlink cut-off Russia kept a 'colossal' lead in fibre-optic drones reaching 50+ km.
After the Starlink cut-off only the deep layer of the Russian kill zone shrank: the satellite-linked strikes 20–200 km deep thinned.
A Russian fibre-optic FPV reached Kharkiv's outskirts on 25 February 2026, showing the fibre layer kept growing.
The ring-wing KVS variant of Russia's KVN fibre-optic FPV carries the same 3 kg payload up to 50 km.
Frontelligence Insight's Tatarigami says about 60% of Russian FPVs in key sectors are fibre-optic (2026).

metric_new.label: Share of drones that are fibre-optic

text: An OSINT tally puts Russian FPV use at about 10,000 a day (2026).
70% of National Guard of Ukraine drones were fibre-optic by September 2026, up from about 20%.

text: ISW, relaying Russian industry sources, reports that Chinese suppliers raised the price of optical fibre for Russian buyers from 16 to 40 yuan per km between early 2025 and early 2026.

text: The struck Russian fibre plant in Saransk had made about 4 million km of optical fibre a year.
Russia's Rassvet satellite constellation had 32 satellites by July 2026.
Rassvet coverage went from 6–10 minute passes in March 2026 to windows of over an hour by late August 2026.
Rassvet has terminals small enough for Geran-type drones.
The 7th Air Assault Corps commander (Pokrovsk axis) described a kill zone 20–25 km deep on both sides of the line in July 2026.
The 7th Air Assault Corps commander expects the kill zone to reach 30 km by the end of 2026.
In the 7th Air Assault Corps sector drones cause 70–80% of damage (July 2026).
In March 2026 Fedorov claimed the Drone Line had 1,000+ crews and made 1 in 4 front-line kills.

observations.subject: Drone Line share of front-line kills

text: In March 2026 Fedorov claimed the Drone Line had struck 10,500+ Russian troops.
In March 2026 Fedorov claimed 33,000+ Russian UAVs destroyed by Ukrainian interceptors.

observations.note: key-figures table gives it as per month

text: In March 2026 Fedorov claimed a 1.3:1 Ukrainian strike-drone advantage over Russia.
In June 2026 Syrskyi claimed a 1.5:1 Ukrainian FPV advantage over Russia.
In June 2026 Syrskyi claimed 12.7% month-on-month growth in Ukrainian drone output from April to May 2026.
Brovdi claimed the USF killed or wounded 102,000 Russians in the 12 months to June 2026.
Brovdi claimed the USF hit 360,000 targets in 1.7 million sorties in the 12 months to June 2026.
Brovdi's USF figures imply about one hit per five sorties, a derived figure that mixes reconnaissance, bomber and strike sorties.

observations.value_text: about one hit per five sorties
observations.note: targets hit per sortie; mixes sortie types

text: Fedorov was dismissed as Ukrainian defence minister on 14 July 2026.
Khmara was appointed Ukrainian defence minister on 19 August 2026.
By September 2026 over 500 Ukrainian units were using DOT-Chain/Brave1 Market and the 'Army of Drones Bonus', against 12 a year earlier.
The e-points scoring economy kept running after the change of defence minister in 2026.
Ukrainian interceptor drone output reached up to 1,000 a day (2026).
Interceptor drones made about 70% of Shahed kills around Kyiv in February 2026.
Of 3,500+ Russian drones downed in May 2026, USF interceptors claimed 1,200+ and helicopters 440+.

Aerial targets destroyed by air defence

text: Beskrestnov said interceptor drones now destroy about 50% of incoming Shahed-types (May 2026), up from about 10% in winter.
notes: Text says interceptors destroy ~50% of incoming Shahed-types; the key-figures table calls it the interceptor share of kills. Ambiguous denominator.

text: Syrskyi warned in 2026 that Russia aims to raise the jet share of its Shahed-type drones to 50%.
The ZIRKA interceptor drone (June 2026) flies at 340+ km/h, costs up to $2,000 and uses AI to detect and track its target automatically.
Monthly Russian Shahed-type launches peaked at 8,161 in May 2026.
The overall Shahed-type hit rate fell from about 16.5% in August 2025 to 6.7% in May 2026.
The Ukrainian Air Force reported 65,618 Shaheds and 10,604 Lancets destroyed from February 2022 to August 2026.

text: From about 5 May 2026 the Ukrainian Air Force stopped consistently publishing Shahed counts, so later monthly figures are reconstructions.
ISIS reconstructs August 2026 as 4,288 Shahed-type drones shot down or suppressed and about 716 hits (13.9%).

metric_new.label: Aerial targets destroyed by air defence

text: ISIS estimates 57–62% of genuine Shahed/Geran use in August 2026 was jet-powered.
Russia launched about 2,800 jet-powered drones in August 2026, up from about 350 in June.
According to Air Force spokesman Ihnat, only about 60% of Russian jet drones are intercepted (August 2026).
In September 2026 Ukraine downed 55% of Russian jet drones, more than 1,500 of over 2,730.

metric_new.label: Aerial targets destroyed by air defence

text: HUR estimates Russia builds about 3,000 Geran-4/5 jet drones a month (2026).
HUR says Russia has stopped making the Geran-3 (2026).
On 6 July 2026 a Russian Molniya with an Nvidia Jetson Orin module picked its own target near a Zaporizhzhia gas station and killed three civilians.
The 6 July 2026 Molniya strike near Zaporizhzhia is the first documented self-targeting Russian drone kill.
Nvidia Jetson modules have turned up in Russian V2U, Lancet and Klin drones since June 2025.
Monthly Ukrainian UGV logistics and evacuation missions rose from 7,511 in January 2026 to 25,143 in August 2026.
Ukraine plans 50,000+ UGVs in 2026.
SkyFall says it makes 100,000 heavy bomber drones a year at $8,500 each.
A SkyFall heavy bomber costs about 16 times as much as an FPV.
A heavy bomber drops three or four grenades a sortie and may fly a dozen sorties before it is lost, so it is cheaper per mission than a one-use FPV.

metric_new.label: UAV life expectancy (flights or sorties before loss)

text: In Operation Vivaldi (Lyman, 3rd Army Corps), heavy bombers air-dropped kamikaze UGVs more than 10 km behind Russian lines.

observations.subject: UGV air-drop depth behind Russian lines

text: The 3rd Army Corps claims Operation Vivaldi cleared 125+ km².
The 3rd Army Corps says Rubikon was pulled from the Lyman sector after losing operators, launch sites and logistics in Operation Vivaldi.
Russia is fielding a Baba Yaga-equivalent heavy bomber called 'Berdysh' and reportedly repairing captured Vampires (2026).

effect: grounds the satellite-linked deep layer; 20–40% effectiveness drop claimed
rationale: The February 2026 whitelist cut Russian terminals; the larger drones that struck 20–200 km deep lost their link, and Biletsky claims a 20–40% effectiveness drop.
Interceptors made ~70% of Shahed kills around Kyiv in Feb 2026 and destroyed ~50% of incoming Shahed-types by May 2026.
Jet Gerans are much harder to intercept: only about 55–60% were intercepted in Aug–Sep 2026.

counter: Ukrainian strikes on drone operators, launch sites and logistics (Operation Vivaldi)
rationale: The 3rd Army Corps says Rubikon was pulled from the Lyman sector after losing operators, launch sites and logistics.

text: Recon quadcopters (DJI Mavic/Matrice, 'mavik', Autel) are used for spotting, adjusting fire and grenade drops, with a typical range of a few km (line of sight), in use since the 2022 invasion.
Recon quadcopters are commercial, mostly built from Chinese parts, and are highly vulnerable to EW through their RF link and GNSS.
Ukrainian fixed-wing ISR drones (Leleka-100, A1-CM Furia, Shark, PD-1, SKIF) are used for ISR, artillery and HIMARS spotting and counter-battery cueing, in service from 2015 (Shark from autumn 2022).
Deviro's Leleka-100 has an 80 km radius, 5 hours' endurance and a 340 km route.
Athlon Avia's A1-CM Furia has a range of at least 50 km, 4 hours' endurance, a 200 km route and weighs 6 kg.
Ukrspecsystems' Shark had a 60 km link and 2+ hours' endurance in 2022.
The Shark-M (2026) has a 180 km link, 7 hours' endurance and a 420 km route.
Ukrainian fixed-wing ISR drones have medium EW vulnerability; makers claim dual anti-jam links and GNSS-free modes.
Russian fixed-wing ISR drones (Orlan-10/30, Zala, Supercam, Eleron) are used for ISR, artillery cueing, laser designation and as an EW payload carrier (Leer-3), in use since the 2022 invasion.
Russian fixed-wing ISR drones reach operational depth, with targets taskable to about 40 km.
Russian fixed-wing ISR drones have medium EW vulnerability and were hunted by Ukrainian interceptor UAVs from 2024–25.
MALE UCAVs (Bayraktar TB2, Orion) were used for long-range strike and ISR from the 2022 invasion.
MALE UCAVs such as the Bayraktar TB2 and Orion have low EW vulnerability but high vulnerability to surface-to-air missiles.
RF FPVs (analog, then digital; 7–10 inch kamikaze quads) are used anti-personnel and anti-vehicle, with a typical range of about 10 km.
An RF FPV costs about $300–400.
RF FPVs were introduced during the Bakhmut period (Dec 2022–May 2023) and used en masse from the Avdiivka period (Oct 2023–Jul 2024).
RF FPVs are highly vulnerable to EW, with 10–15% success under jamming.
AI terminal-guidance FPVs use machine-vision lock-on modules (e.g. ZIR, Skynode) to strike through jamming in the final approach, introduced in 2023–24 with 10,000 bought in 2024.
AI terminal-guidance modules lock on at about 1 km, the ZIR up to 3 km.

Fibre-optic FPVs are immune to RF jamming, but the cable snags or breaks.

FPV-type interceptors are used against Russian Orlan, Zala and Supercam reconnaissance drones for counter-ISR, radar- or electro-optically cued, since Aug 2024–Mar 2025.

Relay or 'mothership' drones (the Molniya FPV carrier, Starlink-fitted Russian drones, repeaters) extend range and carry smaller drones; Russian Starlink-linked drones reached 20–200 km (Mar 2025–Jan 2026).

UGVs are RF-dependent, and Russian UGVs lost Starlink in 2026.

Ukrainian naval drones (Magura V5/V7 of HUR; Sea Baby and underwater Sea Baby of the SBU) are used for anti-ship, anti-tanker, anti-air (with missiles) and submarine strikes, introduced between Dec 2022 and Jul 2024.
